utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is the 16th of October, 2008. Good morning to the accused present, to the Defence counsel, to Mr. Scott and his team, and to all the people helping us out. With regard to the time, you have used one hour and 21 minutes so far, Mr. Scott, so you can add up or take that time off the four hours you were given. So you have two hours and 39 minutes left. We have a short oral ruling regarding the scope of questions dealt with during cross-examination by Ms. Alaburic. The Trial Chamber is of the view that questions that have to do with military strategy are novel questions, are new questions. Therefore, the Trial Chamber will take that into account with regard to the time allotted. This is what we were going to say. You have the floor, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask your leave to say a few words very briefly, up to two minutes, before we continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about? Not to the merits of the case. If it has to do with your health, fine, but not with regard to the case as such, because you're only here to answer questions. What is it about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I actually have an objection to the manner of examination yesterday. I would not say anything about any specific issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So objection to the manner of cross-examination by the Prosecutor. All this is being controlled by the Trial Chamber. As per the Rules, the Judges are the ones that decide as to the way cross-examination or examination is carried out, and they make sure that witnesses are not put under pressure when having to answer questions. We did not notice that there were any pressure exerted on you. You may have perceived or felt that the questions were making you uncomfortable, but that's the way you feel about things. That's subjective. We have to make sure that the examination is not such as to exert pressure or be threatening to you, because if that were to be the case, we would then step in to make sure that the one proceeding in that way stops doing so or there could be a redaction in the LiveNote, but we've not noticed anything of the kind. We've had a few remarks by Mr. Karnavas as to the manner questions were put, but you have the choice. Either you cannot answer a question and you say, "I don't know," or you know and you have to answer the question. There can be no problem, no specific problem or difficulty there for you. Let's proceed. If there were a problem, then you would point it out to us. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to point out to the Trial Chamber, because I do see that one member of the Trial Chamber keeps shaking their head, and there must be an understanding that the gentleman here was a victim, was a victim. And it has been a long-held tradition in this Tribunal, well before any of us came here, that victims are treated differently, irrespective of whether they're Croats, Serbs, or Muslims. Now, even though we're not going into areas regarding how he was treated, and as you may recall, I stayed away from those areas. I did not pander to any emotionalism. I try to keep my -- you know, that's why I asked yesterday if Mr. Scott to modulate his voice and keep in mind that the gentleman was a victim, and that may be something that is causing the gentleman some -- some unease. And I would respect -- I would hope that the Trial Chamber would intervene and not leave it up for me to intervene, because then it gives the impression that I'm trying to protect the witness. And I would like to see equal protection for all victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Mr. Karnavas. This did not escape us. We know that he was a victim because we know that he was detained in the Jablanica museum, and we know, unfortunately, that some of the people very close to him and his family also died. So we take all this in to account. We factor that in, and we know that you have been a victim, as there were, unfortunately, too many of them. So far Mr. Scott has not gone into this topic of victims. I don't know. I can't tell you anything. Let's wait and see. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zelenika.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just very, very briefly say, sir, in light of what has been said, I may at times have put some hard questions to you and, indeed, I may press you rather firmly, and for better or worse, that's the nature of the process. I hold no personal animosity towards you. To the extent that you and your family were victims or may have been victims of the horrible conflict in the former Yugoslavia in which there were victims on all sides, you have my condolences. Sir, you testified yesterday that you never received any salary or money in connection with working for the MUP security station in Jablanica. In that regard, I'd like you please to look at, in your binder, P 10669. Same process that we followed yesterday. P 10669. It's toward the back. I think it's about the eighth one from the back, sir, but unless we've made a mistake, they're in numerical order. 10669.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a record of -- dated the 2nd of April, 1993, from the Jablanica police station, or MUP, being sent to the Mostar police administration, and in this document, I believe you turned to it, if you turn to item number 2, it appears to indicate, sir, does it not, row 2 in the list, your name appears, "Mirko Zelenika." And for the month of March 1993, you were being paid for 23 days; is that correct? Number 2, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed Prosecutor, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what services were you providing to the Jablanica police station in March of 1993 on 23 days for which you were compensated or paid a salary?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not perform any duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you just were paid for 23 days for not doing anything?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We didn't get your answer in the transcript, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes meaning, yes, you received the monies in April 1993 for 23 days in March, but for which, in fact, you say you did nothing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Scott. I look at this document, also at the original, and it has a column for signature --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- which would be the confirmation that the person concerned has, in fact, received something, but it's empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So what -- on what do you base your affirmation that the witness has in fact received something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That he was -- to that extent, Your Honour, I correct my question to suit -- the record indicates that he was to be paid for 23 days. Now, whether it bears a signature that he signed -- that he actually received the money, I agree, Your Honour, that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But, sir, there's a record here, and my point is -- my apologies if I misspoke. It was not intended to misdirect you, sir, but this is a record being sent by the MUP police station in Jablanica to Mostar, to the police administration to be paid -- these are -- attached is the list of members of active and reserve forces of Jablanica police station to be paid their salaries for March 1993, and you are listed as number 2. There is an identification number next to the left -- excuse me, to the right of your name, and then an indication in the column number of days, 23. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the extra microphones be turned off, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dear sir, and I would like to thank you for reminding me, I did say I had done nothing in the police at the time. I was doing something else, and for that something else I was doing, money was brought that should have otherwise been paid to the police, and that's why there is no signature here. I was told that was the money that should have gone to the police, and that's why there's no signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, all right. Thank you for the clarification from all sides, and that's one reason I came back when you said -- you did say earlier that you had not done anything, and now apparently -- are you telling us now that you had done something for which money was being given to you, or at least arranged to be given to you for 23 days in March 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I was doing other jobs that have nothing to do with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, what other jobs were you doing, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was doing some work in the economy regarding the further construction of that Salvation Road that was mentioned previously in my testimony. I was supervising work on the construction of that road, and I was receiving some remuneration, but I knew it was money intended for the police, so I signed a receipt on another list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So you did receive the money then.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in terms of what you were doing at that time, sir, you made a prior statement that, in fact, you were receiving this money because you were active in the political HVO at that time, correct, and throughout this time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. By no means. It was not a political wing of the HVO. I was paid for doing organisational work in the construction of the road that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can go into private session for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we're talking about -- we were talking about 1D 01449, and when that document was shown to you the other day and you opined that it appeared from the document that the HVO did not receive 20 per cent of the meals along this 80 per cent/20 per cent split that we were talking about earlier this week, let me just ask you a couple more questions about that. Prior to the time that Mr. Karnavas showed you that document, 1D 01449, had you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before he showed it to me I -- I had never seen it. I had never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, do you have any personal knowledge, and I'm not asking you to speculate, guess, or state your belief, I'm asking do you have any personal knowledge that the HVO did not, in fact, receive 20 per cent of the meals?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this equal treatment of the HVO in terms of logistics was a constant problem, I can't claim that I know specifically about those 2.500 meals. Maybe I didn't even attend that session. If you asked me whether I attended or not, I wouldn't be able to recall. I cannot remember, although I was a member of the Presidency then, whether I was there when the decision was made on the 2.500 meals, but there was a constant problem enforcing this agreement that 80 per cent should go to the army and 20 per cent to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So your answer, sir -- excuse me, but our time, again, is limited, as you know. So my answer to your question, sir, is that you have no personal knowledge that the HVO did not, in fact, receive meals at that time.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have general knowledge that it did not, but I cannot confirm this specific example, whether it fit into the general picture, because you can see that it was a problem for many other documents. To me it seems irrelevant whether in this specific case it happened that way or not. We have other, many other documents that there was a constant problem with the logistical support to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... how your testimony is received and understood by the Judges in this case? Sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going back to the general --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may just intervene. The record says that the witness said yes, but the witness said yes with a question mark as far as his intonation is concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say yes in confirmation. I said yes, expecting a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I put a question to you, sir, and I'll put it again. You said -- you said something about being -- it seems irrelevant to me. Sir, when you gave that testimony -- see that's my point, sir. When you gave that testimony on Monday, the impression you left with the Judges is that you had -- you had affirmed as if that's something that had really happened, that you had knowledge of that, and now you're saying it's irrelevant to you whether that's true or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but you can't say that the impression that you gave to the Judges, because you don't know what impression he gave us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will say that that is the impression that I perceive that he tried to create and I think I can put that question to the witness. I'm commenting on the witness's testimony and I think I can pursue that. You're right, Your Honour, I can't get into your head, but I think I can put the question to the witness, and he just said it was irrelevant to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He didn't say. Your Honours, I don't want to be disruptive. He didn't say that, and I believe the question is argumentative in nature. So I mean -- if we were in a -- before a jury, this question would be struck down with lightning speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, we're not in front of a jury, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because it's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, it's not. Mr. President, I'm probing the credibility of this witness and I -- it's my perception as one example of an occasion in which a document was put to him that he now tells us he had never seen before and he was asked to opine on it. Now we know that he has no personal knowledge of it and then comes back and says but it's really irrelevant to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question was, so are you saying this is irrelevant. He already answered the question. Now I think the point has been made and the gentleman should just move on. He's made his point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will move on, Mr. President, because I don't want to waste my time -- more of my time on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can go next to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's one question by a Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott. Excuse me. Can we just go back, because you moved very quickly to this document, but I wanted to go back to P 10669 just for a second. Witness, on Tuesday when we were looking at this decision on war tax for citizens, document 1D 01460, I had put a question to you. I had asked you whether the municipality employees or yourself were paid and, if so, in what currency. You answered that municipal employees were not paid at all. Earlier on this morning when we were looking at P 10669 regarding the Mostar police, we found your name in the list of those who were paid, but you explained and I understood your explanation that you were not paid as a policeman but for work that you did with regard to the construction of a road. So let me go back to the question I put on Tuesday. You were paid for this work. So in what currency were you paid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wish to remind everyone that I hadn't been in the municipality as of the 29th October 1992. So I wasn't working in the municipality at all from that time on, but I worked in the civilian HVO doing economic development, road construction, sometimes paid in Croatian dinars, sometimes in German marks. My remuneration would be partly paid in Croatian dinars, partly in German marks one month, another month it would be only German marks, the third month it would be just Croatian dinars. But I did not do that in 1992. In fact, I started in the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed. I can see this document dealing with war taxes. I see the date, 4th of December, 1992. Indeed that the Mostar police, we have the date of the 2nd of April, 1993. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to know whether there is a mistake in the record. Mr. Karnavas has very vigorously said the witness had never pretended that the issue was irrelevant. I find on page 10 of today's record, lines 21 to 23, the following sentence: "To me it seems irrelevant whether in this specific case it happened that way or not." Now, was that wrong? Did you say something different, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot say that I was present at the session when this decision was made. What I did say was that this merely confirms the discrimination of the HVO throughout this period in a number of cases. This is just an illustration, an example. I thought it was just irrelevant whether I was aware of this one single case when I was aware of the practice that was prevalent throughout the year. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just to go back then to the series of events that we were talking about through the second half of 1992 yesterday, and I showed you a number of documents in which I pointed out to you that on a number of occasions the Muslim representatives repeatedly took the position and communicated their position that three ethnic entities were not acceptable, doing things, arranging things on a national basis were not acceptable, for instance, with the military, that they should be based on territorial units and not on ethnicity and I put those question to you. And now following from that, isn't it a fact, sir, that it was because of the Muslims' refusal to go along with Herceg-Bosna and the HVO and the fact that the local HVO leadership apparently had not been able to make that happen, that a number of the Herceg-Bosna HVO leadership were unhappy with the Jablanica HVO civilian and military leadership as it existed at that time, and there was calls for these people to be removed? In other words, that those people, if I can put it in a bit of the vernacular, had not gotten the job done. They had not achieved the Herceg-Bosna agenda. Isn't that what happened at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify a little bit? Who called for the civilian leadership of the HVO in Jablanica to be removed? Who made this demand, because I didn't understand that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look at -- well, let's make it a bit more concrete by looking at Exhibit P 00581 in your binder, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is it approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's the seventh document in the binder, sir, but if you look, sir, by the numbers, you should be able to find all the documents. This is a communication from the military police -- excuse me. My apology. The brigade commander of the Herceg Stjepan Brigade dated the 15th of October, 1992, and during the period that we've been discussing since yesterday. It's addressed to a number of other military police units, Konjic, Jablanica, Mostar, et cetera. And the commander says: "This is to inform you that as of the 17th of October, 1992, all persons in the territory of Konjic and Jablanica that are in possession of a pass allowing them freedom of movement throughout the territory of the HZ HB and the Republic of Croatia shall have their passes authenticated with the Herceg Stjepan Brigade's stamp." Now if we skip a paragraph, the commander then goes on to say: "The reason for taking these measures is abuse of other stamps and they refer to both civilian and military segment of this territory." Now, here again it appears to be that it is the HVO that is asserting the authority to permit or not permit movement in these municipalities, Konjic and Jablanica. Do you recall that at the time, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed Prosecutor, you asked me a little while ago -- or, rather, you wanted me to confirm that there was this initiative to remove the civilian segment of the HVO in Jablanica from office because they were not doing their job right, and now you are showing me a military document, and I can't really understand what it has to do with what you've asked me, and I don't see any civilian HVO mentioned anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look, sir, in the -- if you look in the third paragraph that I read out loud to you a moment ago, it says: "The reason for taking these measures is abuse of other stamps and they refer to both civilian and military segment of this territory. This report has been endorsed with Herceg Stjepan Brigade's stamp so that you may see what it looks like." If that's not clear enough to you, sir, let's move from that. I gave you that as an introduction. Let's move to the next document, P 00582. It should be the very next document in your binder. P 00582 by the same commander the very next day the 16th of October, 1992. And on that occasion, the same commander writes to Mate Boban, Jadranko Prlic, Bruno Stojic, Andjelko Siljeg, and repeats some of the actions that he is taking in the area: "I'm hereby informing you that on 16 October 1992, I was forced, due to their failure to carry out orders, to disband the 3rd Battalion command from the Herceg Stjepan Brigade, Konjic, as well as the HVO Municipal Staff command, Jablanica. "In line with orders issued verbally by Mr. Bruno Stojic, I issued an order in writing that all stamps from the areas of Jablanica and Konjic should be withdrawn and the stamp of the Herceg Stjepan Brigade from Konjic should be regarded as the sole valid one." Skipping a paragraph: "It is necessary in this situation to appoint without delay a new HVO Municipal Staff command and its president as well as other military and civilian bodies in Jablanica. We therefore kindly ask you," Mr. Boban, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, and Mr. Siljeg, "to take appropriate action on your part so that this can be done as soon as possible." Now, you knew, didn't you, that there was dissatisfaction among the HVO, that some of the local military and civilian HVO leadership or officials at that time were viewed as being too cooperative with the Muslims. They had not been able to get Herceg-Bosna established in Jablanica, and people like this commander were acting to have them removed and replaced; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely not correct, sir. At that time I was still the president of the Executive Board of the Jablanica municipality, and I was not in the civilian HVO, and I did not know about this dissatisfaction, although I did see people around, and I was not aware of this initiative that you're talking about to remove people from office, to have them replaced. So I cannot really confirm this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as has been mentioned already today, I regret needing to raise the topic of your brother Marko, but I must in this particular context. What was the position of your brother Marko Zelenika in the HVO in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother was the commander of the Mijat Tomic Battalion, which was active in the Jablanica municipality, and it was part of this brigade, the HVO Brigade Herceg Stjepan that was headquartered in Konjic. He was the commander of the battalions from sometime in July 1992 until the fall of 1992. But please do not ask me to give you a specific date. Sometime in the fall, October or maybe November. I know that this was roughly the time period, from the summer until the fall of 1992. So he was a commander in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was that the 3rd --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Was that the 3rd Battalion of the Herceg Stjepan Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the number designation, but it was designated as Mijat Tomic. Now, I don't know what the numbers were, the 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, again --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but that was its distinguishing feature, its name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, again with my regret for having to raise it, but isn't it a fact that your brother was removed from that position in about January of 1993 because he was perceived to be too cooperative with the Muslims and was removed from his position?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely not correct. I will not get emotional as I was when I read the text and I saw his signature, and that really moved me. What you said is a heinous lie. My brother -- well, it was in the fall or maybe sometime in January around New Year's Day, he got paralysis. One side of his face got paralysed so he went to the hospital in Split for treatment. And yet now we can see that some people tried to foist those terrible lies on you and now you come here and you present them in court here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, whatever physical problems he may or may not have had at that time, sir, and again if that's the case, I regret that. Sir, around that time, at the end of 1992 or early 1993, he was removed, perhaps it was coincidental, perhaps not, he was removed from his HVO position; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not removed, sir, unless there is a document from his superiors to that effect. If you have a document to that effect and if you show it to me, then I will agree with you, but I claim that he was not removed. This is the first time that I hear anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving forward, sir, the efforts of the -- of the Herceg-Bosna authorities and the HVO to again assert control over the Jablanica area, that continued through January, February, March of 1993, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. As far as Jablanica is concerned, there were no such efforts at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For example, around -- in early January 1993, someone who the Chamber has heard, a General Daidza, came to the centre of Jablanica town with HVO soldiers, kind of flexing their muscles in the area; correct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that, but General Daidza led both the HVO soldiers and the BH army soldiers. He had both under his command. I never saw him lead only the HVO troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in the middle of January 1993, and we're not going to go to all of these documents because we don't have time, but the Chamber will recall, and others in the courtroom, that it was on the 15th of January, 1993, that we had certain actions, a decision by Jadranko Prlic, an order by Bruno Stojic imposing a deadline on the 20th of January, 1993, for the ABiH units and areas that were then being called Vance-Owen provinces 3, 8, and 10 to subordinate themselves to the HVO or to leave the areas. Now, did that come to your attention around this time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not the right person to ask this question. You cannot ask me -- ask me this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So this is another one of these topics that you didn't -- you didn't know anything about, these high-level orders coming down from the president of the HVO and the head of the HVO defence department? Never came to your attention?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of it, and I find it strange that you apparently don't realise who I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you can go, please, to P 01164. P 01164. Sir, this is a document issued by -- an order by the HVO military police in Jablanica on the 16th of January, 1993, the day after the Prlic and Stojic documents, and it says in the top: "Pursuant to the order of the Jablanica HVO and the order by the head of the defence department and the military police of the HZ HB, the Jablanica military police is obliged to carry out the following." And I'm not certainly going to go through all of this but number 1: "Population of the Jablanica municipality are allowed to leave the municipality with the appropriate approvals issued by," then it lists the people who can do that. Number 4 [sic]: "The accompanying documentation for arms, military equipment and ammunition imported from the Republic of Croatia or another country" -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to object to the part of the question where the Prosecutor establishes a link between the previous document by Mr. Stojic with this document. In the preamble of this order, which is signed by Mr. Livaja, there is no mention of the reference. So you cannot really see from the text that it had anything to do with the previous order, and the question by Mr. Prosecutor goes as follows: "One day after the order by Mr. Stojic." I think it is very difficult, in fact impossible to establish a link between the documents, both on the basis of the preamble and the text itself, although the Prosecution is apparently trying to do just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, everything I have said is based absolutely on the evidence. On the 15th of January, the head of the HVO department of defence, Mr. Bruno Stojic, in document number P 01140 issued his decision to enforce the Prlic decision of the same date, the 15th of January, 1993. I turn to this document and it says, and I didn't make it up, it says: "Pursuant to the order by the Jablanica HVO and the order by the head of the defence department and the military police of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." So I leave it to Your Honours to draw your own inferences and put the evidence together and draw your conclusions, but it's certainly fair for me to put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was reading, sir, before I was interrupted, on point number 3: "The accompanying documentation for arms, military equipment and ammunition imported from the Republic of Croatia or another country that needs to cross over check-points and the municipality of Jablanica should be signed by the head of the defence department of Herceg-Bosna, HZ HB, Bruno, probably Stojic," and I leave it to the courtroom to look at the document. I don't think it's as illegible as in this particular instance the translator might have. "Bruno Stojic, the chief of the HVO main staff, Milivoj," and I submit that the original shows "Petkovic," et cetera, et cetera. Now, sir, this is a document that was issued on the ground in Jablanica affecting what was happening on the ground in Jablanica in mid-January 1993. Did you see these things -- these sorts of things taking place? Did you see efforts to regulate, by the HVO, who could leave and move about the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was not an effort only on the part of the HVO. I know that even before this time an agreement was in place whilst the check-points were set up that their purpose was to control the traffic of passengers, people, and goods. So what you read to me in this item merely serves to establish control on the passage of persons and goods. This is nothing peculiar. The BH army did this as much as the HVO. So this is not strange at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not strange at all. So you confirm that this is what was happening at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do confirm that the traffic of people and goods was controlled.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there is a mistake here. I hope it's accidental. The document does not know -- does not talk about the passage of people and goods and neither does the previous document that speaks about the replacement of stamps, because the Prosecutor skipped the part where it says that stamps were abused from the previous document. So could we please read what it says in the order. It is indicated that they can move but only pursuant to an approval issued by the Jablanica HVO with the signature and stamp of Matan Zaric. So here we're not talking about the HVO controlling people going in and out, but this is all about the stamp. The reason is because the Prosecutor, I believe it was accidental, in his haste forgot to read the part of the notice that was sent to Mr. Boban, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, and Mr. Sagolj where it says that the stamps are being abused. The whole story here is about the abuse of stamps, the stamps and signatures that make it possible for somebody to get in and out. This is not about the HVO establishing control over who gets in and out of the municipality. I think that this is what arises from the document if you read it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to say something very briefly. If I was following, perhaps this is a problem of translation, when the Prosecutor asked the question, he referred to the previous question and documents that pertain to Jablanica and movements in Jablanica. Now, since I don't have the right to redirect and although in direct there was no discussion about military police and these matters, I would just like to say that we heard Safet Idrizovic, a member of the BH army, here in court, and this goes to the credibility of this witness because the Prosecutor obviously is trying to impeach the witness. Witness Safet Idrizovic at page 9833 of the transcript confirmed the very thing that this witness has been saying. He talked about the check-points and about the joint patrols. In February and March 1993 those mixed patrols were composed of the BH army, BH MUP, and the HVO military police. So in March and February 1993, they had those joint patrols. The witness confirmed it, and a document PD 0227 [as interpreted] was admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, we were about to turn --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- the significance of all that. The documents speak for themselves and I think I accurately presented them to the Chamber, so I'm not really sure what all that was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But in any event, sir, let's move forward to the appoint of Mr. Cibo, who you've talked about quite extensively. Do I understand your position on this to be, sir, that there was some sort of a -- my -- my characterisation, but some sort of a Muslim plan or programme by which Mr. Cibo was sent and controlled by Mr. Izetbegovic in Sarajevo to carry out some particular agenda, if you will, in the Jablanica area? Is that basically what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see the plan. What I did see were some consequences of the plan. But after the war, after my detention, I got hold of some documents, and I realised that all those documents taken together show that there was this plan that Mr. Cibo should come to Konjic and Jablanica to stir trouble among Croats and Muslims and to bring war into Konjic, Jablanica, and Herzegovina as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, sir, if I -- again if I misspoke or misdirected you, I apologise. I didn't say if you saw a plan in terms of a written plan. I was just trying to understand. It's your basic position that Mr. Cibo was sent by Sarajevo with a programme. That's your position; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it your position -- or it has been stated in this courtroom that Sarajevo was cut off. Can you tell us how it was that these communications or coordinations were taking place between what was happening in Jablanica and the direction that you said was coming from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the communication went underneath the tunnel that was dug beneath the runway at Sarajevo airport. That was in autumn 1993. That was the only way in which it was possible to establish this communication from Jablanica to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And so you're telling the Chamber that this programme was being carried out and coordinated by Sarajevo with Mr. Cibo and others in Jablanica, and the sole way that that was being done was by communications carried through the tunnel at the Sarajevo airport. Is that what you're telling the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot now say that it was impossible to travel in some other way, perhaps by helicopter. What I do know, however, is that there was this tunnel. It is possible that some people travelled by helicopter too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've then gone on to say, if I understand your position, that Mr. Izetbegovic appointed Cibo. I think what you've said in your testimony in the last couple of days was contrary to -- something to the effect contrary to the laws and practices. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, in particular, the particular aspects in which you say that Mr. Cibo's appointment was contrary to law and customary practice at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The regulations, the laws regulating the procedure for the appointment of the local authorities in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that were in force stipulated that in order for somebody to be elected the president of the municipality and for members of the Municipal Assembly to be elected only persons who had permanent place of residence in that particular municipality could be put on the slate. And based on the election, those representative bodies in the municipality was set up. They were called the municipal assemblies. And in the case of Jablanica, in our case, the Assembly had 35 representatives. And then at a session of this Assembly, the president was elected by a majority of votes. And in this manner, in 1992, Sefer Hamdo was appointed or elected the president of the Municipal Assembly by a majority of votes. And then later on in 1992, he was replaced by Mr. Nijaz Ivkovic who was also a representative, one of the elected representatives. So it was impossible. The law did not provide for a possibility for somebody from another municipality on anyone's decree, on anyone's decision, to be appointed the president of the Municipal Assembly. So I can only repeat what I've already said. This was simply unconstitutional, unlawful, illegal. This was a political and a legal precedent. And Muslims in Konjic and Jablanica opposed it most of all, and everybody realised that this was chaos. It was a chaotic situation. Anything went in that state, because you could bring in people from other municipalities to be presidents of the municipality -- of another municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was the Municipal Assembly in Jablanica meeting in March, April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in the municipality then, but I don't believe they convened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that especially in wartime or crisis situations much of decisions -- many decisions like these get made by political agreement?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not a political agreement. It was a case of imposing someone against everyone's political will. You could see that those people in Konjic were up in arms against it. This decision to replace Mr. Ivkovic came to Jablanica with the signature of Mr. Izetbegovic, and I was invited to the SDA and they showed it to me. It was not along the Presidency line. It was along the SDA line to replace Nijaz Ivkovic. We asked the Muslims in the SDA board, "What are you going to do about this?" They said, "This is not going to pass, no way. We are going to oppose this."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir. Sir, the position you held in Jablanica municipality between April 1992 and the end of October 1992, you did not hold that position lawfully, isn't that true, because you were never approved by the Assembly? You told us that in your testimony on Monday. You got your position as a result of a political agreement which was never approved by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something entirely different, and I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go, please, to Exhibit P 10668. P 10668.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If the gentleman wishes to explain, he should be given the opportunity to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott. He wants to provide an explanation. What did you mean to say, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The fact is the Prosecutor tried to compare two completely incomparable things. I came to the position of the president of the Executive Board of Jablanica on the 11th of May, 1992, based on a decision by the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff was an operative body which under the peculiar circumstances of the immediate threat of war had all the powers of the Assembly, the same powers as the Assembly. Anything that the Crisis Staff decided was legal, and once an opportunity arises, the Crisis Staff was under obligation to submit it's decisions to the Assembly. The first discussion of my appointment was sometime in June, and it was at a time when the Crisis Staff filed to the Assembly all the decisions, appointments, et cetera, it had enacted between April and June. Some of those were verified by the Assembly, others were rejected. Nobody said I was an illegal appointment, an unlawful appointment. I was chosen by a body which had the legal right and basis to appoint me. So my case cannot be compared in any way to the case of Mr. Cibo who was practically imposed against everyone's will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I won't repeat and go back to your testimony on Monday about that. Everyone will have that. Because that's not what you said at the time. Sir, let me ask you to go to P 10668. P 10668. Toward the back of the binder, please. I think Mr. Karnavas may have shown you a similar document by a -- with a Defence number, so I don't think it will be new to you, but it's also been -- well, in any event. P 10668. Sir, this appears to be the decision of the, among other things, appointing Mr. Cibo in Article XV to -- and concerning Jablanica, and Article XVI concerning Konjic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: XV and XVI, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Just so there's no misunderstanding, if we go back to the top of the first page of the document, this reflects that this action was taken at the session of the 13th of March, 1993, the Presidency, I emphasise the word "Presidency," not President Izetbegovic. "The Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted the following." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you could next go to Exhibit P 10667. It should be very close to the one you were just looking at. P 10667 is a decision in which Mr. Cibo was dismissed from that position or those responsibilities, and that document --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. I haven't found it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The one before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It should be the one right before it, sir. They're in numerical order.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 667, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And, sir, would you agree with me that this action was taken, and I'm again directing your attention to the preamble, if you will. This was taken action at a session on 14 December 1993, the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina issued the following decision, and then et cetera. It speaks for itself, giving recognition to Mr. Cibo and essentially dismissing him from those responsibilities. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I think for the interest of time -- thank you, sir. I'd like to direct your attention next to the topic -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. There is a problem of semantics, because the Prosecutor has just said that he is dismissed of his duties, dismissing in English. He was dismissed. But there's no mention of dismissing in the document. It says that the work is being ended because the reasons that had been that he was appointed no longer are present. So in your view, Witness, is it that he was dismissed because he had made a mistake, or he no longer does the job because there is no reason for him to continue doing the job? What is your view on this? Or maybe you have no opinion whatsoever, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was not dismissed in that sense, Your Honour. He was relieved of his duties because he has done the work he was supposed to do. He had organised in Jablanica a dozen of camps through which more than 3.500 Croat civilians and defenders passed through. He organised the ethnic cleansing of 11.500 Croats in the territory of Jablanica and further afield. He organised the persecution of Croat civilian population, and that's why the reasons for his existence in Jablanica ceased. One more thing is said here in paragraph I. A term is used, "Commissioner," and the municipality of Prozor is mentioned. But you have seen in these documents, although from my point of view they are unlawful and unconstitutional, that those who enacted them thought otherwise. Dr. Cibo was not, according to these documents, in charge of Prozor municipality because I personally read in Muslim press that Cibo was the president for Jablanica and for Konjic and for 20 per cent of the territory of Prozor. So that's my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to the question of -- well, some of the questions that you -- things that you say took place in Jablanica in or around the period of April, May thereafter. One question I'd like to touch on just before we go forward. You talked about the electrical power being disconnected to some parts of Jablanica municipality. On that general topic, sir, isn't it correct that it was the HVO who cut off the electrical and water supply from the west to Sarajevo and Konjic during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which year are you talking about? You said April, May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me come back to you. I was going to turn, sir, to the time that some things happened and through the summer when you're talking about -- when you were mobilised for labour, and I did jump to that, sir, you're absolutely right, but you had also -- before I got to that -- what I was doing was amending my sequence, sir, so if I misled you I'm sorry. Before I get to that I would like to come to your testimony about electrical power, because you raised that and were talking about -- and how it was cut off and how Izetbegovic supposedly said something about it. Isn't it correct, sir, that it was the HVO who cut off the electrical and water supply coming from the west of Sarajevo, cut off the electrical and water supply to Sarajevo and Konjic during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I lived in Jablanica. I cannot talk about electricity and water in Sarajevo. I can tell you about the electrical power and water in Jablanica if you have anything to ask me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Jablanica town had electrical power through the war, throughout the war? Is that right? I'm not saying there may have not been a day here and a day there, but generally had power throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Jablanica town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the Croat-controlled areas of Jablanica municipality, they had electrical power during most of the war. Perhaps not from Jablanica, but by one means or another that they were provided with electrical power during most of the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that area where the Croats were under the control of the HVO did not have a single day during the war and quite a long time after the war when they had electricity. Twenty-two months in total. We organised another supply of electrical power through another channel from the hydro power station elsewhere, because they -- it was no longer available from Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When was the power arranged from the hydro power station elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That arrangement was made -- in fact, it began in 1994 after I personally came to meetings in Jablanica from Mostar and begged, implored people in the Muslim leadership to release electricity. And when I was absolutely certain, when they convinced me that they wouldn't do it, I had no choice but to pass on their decision. And we had to make a decision to build a completely new transition line from the hydro power station Rama.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to your mobilisation for work. And again, sir, as I touched -- as I get into this topic, I'm sorry if it might seem like prying to you, but sometimes in these cases we pry a bit more than perhaps we would in everyday, polite conversation. You've talked about some sort of a medical element or disability. Can you -- is there a particular diagnosis that you were ever given for that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us what it is, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was osteomyelitis femoris dex. In a normal language it's inflammation of the femur. I suffered from that for the first time as a boy. I was hospitalised for the same reason in Sarajevo, in Kraljevica, and later in Croatia. Because of that condition I also changed school. I had originally started training for electricians, but I did my military service and after serving in the army in 1973 my situation deteriorated. I was sent to the military medical panel in Mostar. They decided I was no longer fit to serve any further in the army. They said I should avoid long walks, standing for a long time. I was unfit for marching or guard duty. And based on that, the secretariat for general administration in Jablanica adopted in 1973 the decision that I was unfit for military service, so I was assigned to civilian protection, and I was the commander of the Municipal Board for civilian protection. With such a medical file and with the decision from the municipality, that same Secretariat for National Defence summoned me 20 years later to take a pick and an axe and a shovel and report for duty. I rejected that. They sent the police to fetch me by force and bring me there, and I showed the relevant decision to the secretary of the secretariat, and I told him, "Mr. Omer, you have this same decision in your archive. How could you send me the summons, the call-up?" He told me, "None of that that was issued earlier no longer applies. There will be a revision, but until the revision you have to respond to the call-up." And I went every day to dig trenches, to fell trees, cut timber. And when the invitation to revision arrived, the doctors at the hospital didn't even look at me, because Cibo ordered them to disregard the oath of Hippocrates. Now that Cibo was there, the doctors only had to obey. I was before a panel of seven medical doctors. All of them had given the oath and they had to disregard it and dismiss all medical reasons, and I had to go to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It may be of some assistance, Your Honour, given the question what he suffered. The gentleman did provide to the Prosecution back in 1996 a document which has the ERN 00388360. We could put it on the ELMO, and it quite clearly states what the gentleman -- it's a medical report. It's the actual medical report, and perhaps this could be shown to the gentleman. We could put it on the ELMO and it could be seen that this is from 22/11/1973, and it does have the Latin term for the actual diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question isn't if that's the case at all. I'm simply was -- I thought it might be interesting since we've heard all this testimony but we'd never actually gotten the underlying information. I just simply thought that was something that we might want for the record, but I never put into question the 1973 diagnosis, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We may need to get an IC number for this, too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have an IC number, Mr. Registrar, for this medical document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be IC number 863. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The board, sir, that you said, and I think it's probably implied but again because of just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm a bit puzzled by the Defence during cross-examination introducing a document, but I think it would be the least that the witness looks at it and confirms that it is what it's purported to be. Usher, can you show it to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Judge Trechsel is right. Now we're going to waste some minutes on this. Is this your medical report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is the finding of the medical panel. And I told you in my own words what it says with 80 per cent accuracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, it was so obvious that I hadn't even thought that it was necessary to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That was my reaction as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The board that made the original decision in 1973, because you referred to -- you were then named or made the head of the Civilian Protection Board, if I understood you correctly. Maybe I got it wrong. But I understood that you said you were made the head or referred to the Civilian Protection Board back at that time, and I take it that was also Jablanica municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And if I can ask you, please, to look at P 10672 in your binder. P 10672.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 0672, or 672 are the last numbers.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, this particular document is dated the 25th of June, 1993, titled "General mobilisation call-up." And says: "For the purpose of the replenishment of the municipality work unit," at least that's the way it's been translated, "conscript Mirko Zelenika is hereby called up to report to the terrace outside of the municipal -- municipality building ..." et cetera, et cetera. Now, is this the kind of document that you received around this time that you've been telling us about, sometime during 1993 to report for a work detail?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I only took one summons. It doesn't mean I was called up on the 26th June for the first time. I was called up for the first time back on the 15th of April. But I saved just one call-up paper as an example of the abuse of the work obligation. In fact, it was forced labour. And for these reasons that I stated, I was not liable to be called up --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for work obligation, let alone for forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're jumping ahead of me. You're assuming things that I'm not putting to you. I didn't suggest this was the first time, but is this an example of the kind of document that you received in connection with being called up for work?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you receive such a document on -- on only one occasion or more than that and, if so, approximately how many times did you receive the document? I mean approximately. I mean just -- are we talking about once or twice or every day or 50? Give the Judges some idea of how often did you receive a document like this.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Constantly went to do that forced labour beginning with the 15th of April, and they only sent documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me. Sorry to interrupt you but, again, our time is limited. I didn't ask you if you went every day. My question is how often would you receive a document like this? Did you receive one every day?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have another document with the same language, but it was sent by the Executive Board. The Executive Board over which I presided sent the same call-up except the signature was the president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, perhaps that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then I know we're coming up to the break, Your Honour, but if we could finish with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps that's the exhibit which is right before that one which is P 10671. Do you see that? It should be the one right before it, sir, 10671.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one. That's the document that I was talking about. It's the very same document. As you see, it's only the president of the Executive Board here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. And before we take the break, sir, can you just -- so are you telling us then that from -- because I heard you say a few moments that you -- you first reported for work or did work, at least if I understood you correctly, on the 15th of April, and is that -- is that correct? Is it on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how often did you engage in this sort of a work detail between the 15th of April, 1993, and the time that you were unfortunately taken into the camp, as you've told us, in, I don't know, early September 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I went every day. There are only two days that I didn't go. It was the 12th and the 13th of June, the two days when I went to attend the meeting at Mr. Safet Cibo's. So only the 12th and the 13th of June I didn't go. I went every day until the 8th of September. Actually, I went there also on the 8th of September, the very day when I went to the camp later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think we can stop here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, we have something to ask from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Not only me but also colleagues of mine have wondered where you were going with this health issue and forced labour. We do not quite understand the relevance. Perhaps you will tell us that it's testing credibility and then, of course, that will be it, but could you enlighten us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I guess two responses, Your Honour. As to the first point, I did simply think that since there had been questions about medical health, that we get a -- if there had ever been a diagnosis that we ever actually get a diagnosis. I thought that seemed to be appropriate. Maybe I was the only one that was curious. If so -- secondly, Your Honour, if -- I do have a few additional questions about it and I think it is relevant to the nature of what this witness calls forced labour and the characteristics of it. So if I'm ultimately wrong, of course, the Chamber's not persuaded it's relevant, I guess I've wasted my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in terms of -- or I guess I should say, if I can -- Judge Trechsel, if I can respond one moment further. Of course I can't know what the Chamber thinks of the evidence so far, so I can't -- perhaps you're already ahead of me. Maybe you are, maybe you're not. It leaves all counsel in the -- I'm sure Mr. Karnavas and others, sometimes not being sure of where the Chamber might be on particular evidence. In looking at -- and I'm just using as an example, sir, that -- I tell you right now that there's nothing magical about this particular 10672, just as the document itself. It says: "General mobilisation call-up," and I guess in response to Judge Trechsel's question, this was -- whatever your own personal difficulties, again, sir, which we can all regret, this was a civilian protection work detail that people from all over Jablanica town, both Croats and Muslims, were called out to do work, public work, in this way; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. All the people, Croats and Muslims alike, who were healthy and who were within a certain age bracket, who were not children, who were not the elderly, could -- or, rather, had to respond to this call-up. But persons such as myself could not be summoned to do this kind of work. There wasn't a single law that provided for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, sorry, again, sir, if my question wasn't clear, but I think you did answer my question. The intent of my question was this was not something imposed on you as a prisoner or a detainee. It wasn't just imposed on Croats. The able-bodied people in Jablanica, be they Croat or Muslim, were mobilised for these work details throughout this time period; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, sir. Croats were mobilised to do this kind of work, to dig trenches, to carry ammunition and food to the combat positions and to cut timber, and Muslims got tasks to clean the roads, to load and unload. They never carried ammunition and food to the front lines. And there was a law stipulating that only those who were able to perform a certain task, who were in good health could be summoned, and there was no law in Bosnia and Herzegovina that stipulated that I, with the condition that I had, could be summoned to do the kind of work that I, in the end, had to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as one of my colleagues likes to say, work with me on this for a moment. I'm not asking you -- I'm putting aside your personal situation, all right, and your personal hardship and your physical problem, and I -- again, we all regret that. Putting aside your particular situation. If you will -- if you'll allow me, I'm talking now more general, and I was reacting specifically, sir, to your testimony a few moments ago, and it's just about to leave the page, it just did leave. Page 41, line 3. You said all people, all the people, Croats and Muslims alike, were called out to engage in what I've called a public work -- public works, public work details. Now, let's start with that. That's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. This is the third time that I'm telling you this. Croats were sent to do forced labour, and Muslims were given tasks that could be subsumed under work obligation. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, again, one step at a time. I understand -- you're loud and clear that your position is that Croats were sent for a particular kind of work and Muslims were engaged in a different type of work. I have you on that. But in general when these -- these generalisation -- these generalisation mobilisation call-up, the type of thing that we see in Exhibit P 10672 and P 10671, these were mobilisations for all the people, able bodied people living in Jablanica, both Croat and Muslims. That's my only question to you at the moment. If you can assist us, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me assist you in this way: While I was mobilised, as is indicated in the call-up paper, there were never any Muslims doing this kind of work. And I do know that they went to do other work, easier tasks, ordinary tasks. And I knew everybody there. Over the four months there was not a single Muslim who worked with me. And I do know that they went to do other kinds of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you have not received, of course, the answer to your question precisely, but I think implicitly you have, and I would suggest that you not insist now, because the experience shows that it will be probably not very fruitful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's exactly what I was going to do. I think that -- I hope that the Chamber -- once again, I can't assert, as the President reminded me this morning, I can't know what's in the Judges' heads, of course, but hopefully the point's been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, in terms of -- now, I'm accepting what you're saying. You're saying the Croats were sent to do a particular kind of different work. So I'm on the same page with you, okay? But when you say you went -- that you did these other tasks, can you tell us the locations? Will you tell us some of the locations that you were sent to do these other tasks and what you actually did there? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to a location. It's elevation Pisvir in the direction of Poljane, in the direction where the HVO positions were. We carried food and ammunition and we dug trenches there. We went to Boksevica too. Again, in the direction where the HVO positions were, we carried food, ammunition and water and we dug trenches. We also went to the Prenj mountain where we cut timber for the fortifications of the BH positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we went to Mount Prenj --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not trying to be impolite but I'm trying to manage my time. And I agree with that. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say that you went to cut timber and dig trenches and did these things, how close were you to the actual confrontation line when you did these things?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were very close. People were killed on those lines. Fortunately, I survived. And people, some were wounded in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And so I take it -- that was my next question, and I think it was as Judge Trechsel would say, it's implicit, but just to make it very clear. So on some occasions when you were engaged in this work, it was -- combat was active. Fighting was going on. Is that -- are you telling us that, or did I misunderstand?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you consider it improper, sir, inappropriate for you and the other Croats who were taken and used in that way? Did you consider that to be improper behaviour?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I thought it was against some law somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question, Mr. Witness. The front line, who was on the other side? Who was the enemy on the other side of the line? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was the HVO army that was on the other side as the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I am leaving that topic unless the Judges -- I'm leaving that topic unless the Judges have other questions about that. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to be handed now before we proceed, in light of testimony earlier today, if the witness could please be provided -- it's not in the binder but I've asked to be distributed P 01631. Defence counsel, I think, all have it, and if it could be given to the Chamber if they don't have it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And while that is happening, Your Honour, I'm told that there may be a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was going to deal with that, Counsel. Yes, I'm aware. Thanks to Ms. Alaburic. As Mr. Karnavas said, there may be a translation question which I am grateful to Ms. Alaburic for bringing it to my attention, which I'll get to in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But, sir, if you have that document which is P 01631, this appears to be a document, an HVO record dated the 9th of March, 1993, over the name of Bruno Stojic with a stamp of the Herceg-Bosna Mostar stamp on it, which appears to be, and again, if it's difficult for you, I again regret having to bring up the topic of your brother, but it appears to relate to your brother Marko Zelenika. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, in terms of the potential translation issue, and I'll ask for the assistance of the booth, please, if you can read for us where it's -- where it says "Command" in your language and under -- immediately below "Command." If you could please read that slowly enough so the translation booths can assist us in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I read the whole text or just where it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- order?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can help you further, help all of us. The top of the document goes on with a preamble, and then it says: " ... hereby issues the following command," or order, what have you. And immediately following -- so if you'd find that portion. Can you start reading where it says: " ... hereby issues the following," and then read that, you know, next seven or eight, ten words, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Order to discharge from the position in the Herceg Stjepan Brigade in Konjic." Under number 1: "Marko Zelenika is discharged from the position of the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the Herceg Stjepan Brigade, Konjic. The defence office, personal military speciality establishment, military speciality establishment, rank, addressees."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The operational zone commander, the unit, the personnel department, and the chief -- and the General Staff of the HVO."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. Can you tell us -- well, did you know anything about this order? I'm not asking if you'd seen the particular document, but did you ever learn, around March or the spring of 1993, about the discharge of your brother, Marko Zelenika, from the post of commander of the 3rd Battalion by Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about this discharge. I didn't know who issued it, and I didn't see this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Can I turn to the topic, please, of the use of your flat. If I understand your testimony correctly, you testified that sometime in mid-April -- in the second half of April 1993, a Muslim family was put up in your flat in Jablanica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, is it correct, sir, that by the second half of 1993 -- well, excuse me. Let me restate that. Can you assist us with approximately how many Croat civilians were still in Jablanica town by the latter part of April 1993? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the seat of the municipality in Jablanica there were over 500 Croats, but we should also take into account those who had been expelled from the villages around it and came to the capital of the municipality. So there were about 500 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
