utterances.text: All right. I didn't qualify my question in any way, sir. I just wanted how many -- your estimate of approximately how many Croat civilians were in Jablanica town by the latter part of April, and you say about 500.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us when this Muslim family was put into your flat how -- how that was arranged, how that came about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done pursuant to an order of the War Presidency stipulating that everybody was under an obligation to take in a family of displaced persons, but the way it was implemented was that only Croat and Serb families had to do it, whereas Muslim families did not have to put up any displaced persons' families.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again so the record is very clear, what you're saying was that the regulation or the programme, if you will, was supposed to apply to everyone, including Muslims, but you're saying was implemented in such a way that it was only Croat and Serb - excuse me - householders or families that, in fact, did so or were required to do so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could I ask you, please, to look at P 10673. It should be toward the end of the binder, I would think, somewhere. 10673. Fifth from the back, I'm told. Is this a copy of the document, sir -- it's titled on the top of the page, at least in translation, as "Contract on joint use of flat." Is that the document that you were involved in, in terms of this family being placed in your flat?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just one or two questions. In terms of the people -- the distribution list at the bottom of -- I think it's on the second page in both events. Yes. Number 3, Jablanica Public Utilities Enterprise; number 4, Elektro-Jablanica Power Company. I'm just curious as to -- do you know why the document was provided to the public utilities enterprise and the power company?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed Prosecutor, I'm extremely happy that this document is here. I'm overjoyed, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad I could assist you in that way, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really overjoyed, because this document is written in my hand. This is my handwriting. These are the names of the people who, pursuant to the decision of the War Presidency, were put until my apartment, and the procedure for this was as follows: An official of the municipality, in this case it was Sead Bukva, and a police officer would come to your door. They would bring this family with them, and they would tell you, "Mirko, well, this family here has been assigned to your apartment. Please don't let there be any problems." And I accepted that. Sead came later and demanded that I draft this contract, which is what I did, but I never heard of anyone else in Jablanica drafting a contract of this kind. Do you know why I did it? This woman, Bulka Bukva and her daughter and son-in-law Hamdija and the son Mujo and the sister-in-law and two children. The first family had one child, so it's actually three families who had come in from Rogatica to Jablanica in 1992. They had been expelled by the Serbs, and they were in the local cinema. That's where they were put up. And now when the war broke out between the BH army and the HVO, some of the families, not all of them, were moved out from the collective lodgings to better accommodation. And since Mrs. Bulka had her brother -- her husband's brother, Mujo Bukva, he was -- he lived on the first floor of my building and I lived on the third floor, and Sead did not take this family to Suljo's place, which would have been normal, but he took them to Mirko's apartment. And then in order to secure their status in the future at the time when the war was over, he asked me to write this kind of a contract. But fortunately I knew how to do it, although I'm not a lawyer, but I was able to draft this kind of contract. And I was in this apartment up until sometime in August while there was enough food, and then they evicted me. And I went one street down to Pera Bilica Street, to my parent's place at number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I haven't wanted to interrupt you, but let's again take it in a bit smaller pieces. My specific question to you at this particular point is I see, then, that you -- you thought to send a copy of this to the Jablanica Public Utilities Enterprise and Elektro-Jablanica, and I'm just -- my question to you some minutes ago was why did you distribute this document to them?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Sead Bukva actually dictated this text to me. He was an official of the municipality. He was in this staff for the accommodation of refugees that we've been mentioning so often. And Sead, I guess, thought, or at least that's what he told me, that I should write this. Well, he must have known why this was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, you said that this was -- this programme, decision or programme, whatever it was, that came from the municipality to house people, that this was not -- this was not applied to Muslims, and I want to be sure here that --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're absolutely sure that no Muslims in Jablanica town in 1993 put up refugees or displaced persons in their houses?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot vouch for what happened after I left, after the 8th of September, but while I was there I can state that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me briefly ask you about a document that Mr. Karnavas showed you. I believe you won't have it. It's not in my binder, I don't believe. Perhaps we can have the assistance of e-court because it was a Defence exhibit. 1D 00772. I guess it is. I'm told it is in the back of the binder, sir. So -- third from the back, 1D 00772. This is the -- this was a decision by -- apparently by Mr. Cibo on the 29th of July, 1993, which you essentially dismissed as -- I think you said something like it was nonsense in your testimony the other day, and my question to you, sir, again is similar to some of the other questions I've asked you. Whatever you view of it might be, do you have -- do you have personal knowledge that, in fact, none of the Croats from Doljani took advantage of this situation to move into different accommodations? Do you know for a personal -- out of personal knowledge that no Croat families, in fact, did that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I came into the museum on the 4th of November. These people were already in the museum at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's not my question.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And since I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Hold on a second. Just -- again, my time is limited. My question to you is -- my question to you is, because you dismiss the document and you gave us some reasons for that, but what I'm asking you about now is -- because, again, it's like the documents -- some of the other documents I have asked you about. Whether your personal belief or you don't like the document or what happened around the time, but do you have personal knowledge, sir, that during this time, during the summer of 1993, none the Croats from Doljani took advantage of this situation or the opportunity, what you want to call it, to move into different accommodation? And you either know or you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, isn't it correct that the general conditions in Jablanica town by June, July, August 1993, the conditions there were very difficult for everyone in the town, Muslims, Croats, if there were any Serbs left, I don't know, but it was a bad situation for everyone who was still living in the town; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. The situation was difficult for everyone, but it was extremely difficult for Croats and Serbs who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough. It was very difficult for everyone, according to you more difficult for some than others, but overall it was not a very happy or pleasant situation; correct? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the housing situation which had caused, for example, the -- this family to have to move in with you in April, would it be fair to say, sir, that the housing situation as -- over the course the summer, became even worse?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but, again, not for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And because -- for example, by July and August, isn't it correct that there were Muslim refugees and displaced persons arriving in Jablanica from places like Doljani and Stolac and Capljina, from Prozor and Mostar? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And there came a time, is it correct, that the authorities in Jablanica town decided that because of the housing shortage some families -- families who had more than one flat or house, if you will, the families would move in together into one flat so that another flat could be made available to some of these displaced persons or refugees? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. You said -- you said families that had more than one flat or house. I had only one flat, and everybody else were -- was in the same situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Again perhaps, sir, it's a language issue or perhaps I didn't choose my words wisely enough. When I say "family," now, I'm talking about, for example, your parents -- your parents and yourself. Your parents lived in a house, in a flat, if you will. They had a house. You and your immediate family had a flat. And did it come about during the summer of 1993 that you and your parents moved in -- you moved into your parents' house under a programme to make other flats -- so to make your flat and other flats available to these other persons? That's what was happening; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am one family. My parents are another family. My brother had his own family. But I was expelled, my brother was expelled, and we had to go back to our parents' house after so many years. So we're talking about three families here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. But, sir, I want the Court to understand, because we talk about a lot of things in this courtroom, about ethnic cleansing and forcible transfers and expulsions, et cetera, in a lot of different context. What you're saying here is you were required to move out of your own flat, if I can put it that way, your immediate family's flat, and move back in with your parents in Jablanica town; correct? I'm just trying to be clear, sir, so that we know what exactly happened.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be very clear. Suada, Bulka's daughter told me, "Mirko, this morning the police said make sure you're not in this apartment any more from this day on." And in order not to expose my life to any risk because there were Mujo and Hamdija who were armed members of the BH army, I complied with her order and indeed I never went back to my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, your flat was a flat belonging to the social property, or was it your own house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, Your Honour, all apartments were socially owned. Nobody in Jablanica had privately owned apartments. There were privately owned houses though.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. And again, don't misunderstand me. I'm not saying it wasn't an unpleasant situation, but I do want to be very clear about exactly what it was that happened. And that, again, was something that was happening across the town of Jablanica because of the severe housing problem, and it was happening to everyone; correct? Muslims, Croats, everyone had to make adjustments, as difficult as they were, to provide housing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, I really have to object. I simply can't stay quiet with this way of examination. The Prosecutor now wants to proclaim this expulsion from the man's apartment legal and lawful. It's the same thing that happened in Mostar, which the Prosecutor calls ethnic cleansing. I really don't see the point in asking the witness to qualify his expulsion from his own apartment as something legal and acceptable. I as Defence counsel in this courtroom can simply not take this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us not get into this discussion. Your objection has been recorded in the transcript. Please continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't take a position one way or another. I've been simply putting questions to the witness to describe what happened, and I don't understand -- I don't understand counsel's issue. Maybe there's a translation problem when it goes into Croatian, I don't know. I simply asked the witness to be very specific as to what happened so the Chamber knows when it considers this evidence exactly the nature of what was done. I think it's clear to everyone in the courtroom now than it might have been an hour ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, turning to the museum, sir, which has come up in your testimony, and the people who were staying at the museum. There were two groups of people at the museum; correct? There were people who were civilians, and again perhaps -- not perhaps, undoubtedly in very difficult circumstances, but there was a group of civilians who were at the museum, and then there was also a much smaller group of what we might call prisoners of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And during the time that you were staying at the museum, once you began your time there, and again as unfortunate as that was, approximately how many civilians, putting aside the prisoners of war now, and you can work with me on this, how many civilians were living at the museum at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there were over 500 people in the museum. Five hundred only civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And approximately how many of those were Muslims and how many were Croat?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any Muslims. I only know about Croats. Two hundred fourteen from Doljani, 35 from Grabovica, 20-something from Donja Grabovica, 180 from Konjic, around 70 Croats who had been expelled from apartments in Jablanica and surrounding settlements, and there were even accidental passers-by who were going from Bosnia towards the sea. They were stopped, and when their IDs were checked somebody thought they were Croats mistakenly, and there were actually some Serbs among them. Those are the people I can remember at this moment. And in that basement there were 88 persons who were classified as prisoners of war, 22 of which escaped. And then Zuka sent some men to that cell from which the -- this number had escaped. Those are the approximate numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you please turn to Exhibit P 06528. P 06528.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that? 6528.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There should be a translation there for you. At least I have one here. This is an ECMM report dated the 8th of November, 1993, and if I can direct your attention, please, to -- fortunately the paragraphs are numbered, so if I can ask you to go to paragraph number 5 under the heading "Humanitarian."

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't have the Croat translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It should be -- it's right there, sir. I'm looking -- I see it there.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean here on the screen. Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Number 5, please. This ECMM -- in this ECMM report, the ECMM monitor says: "M1 visited the refugee and POW camp in the Jablanica museum where conditions were described as appalling. Over 600 refugees (Muslim and Croat) are accommodated in the building in addition to 41 Croat prisoners in five cells. There is an urgent need for supplies, in particular, clothing." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you disagreeing with this report that these 600 refugees who were housed at the school [sic] included both Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, only when I got out of the camp, since it was impossible for me to move away from that room where I was held, I hadn't been out of there for four months, I couldn't know what was up there in the museum. But when I got out of the camp, I found out that in the museum there had also been Muslim refugees from Stolac, but they were refugees, whereas the Croats were captives. It's not the same category.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So our problem has been the characterisation of not who was there but apparently some were refugees and, according to you, some were captives. So at the school -- putting that aside for the moment then -- excuse me, at the museum. At least we have -- apparently we have corrected one potential disagreement. You agree that at the -- at the museum there were both Croats and Muslims being housed there, living there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I reject the characterisation "housed." One are captives, the other one are there as refugees. There's quite a bit of a difference. They're not living there as is being suggested. Let's be precise with our language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm trying to simply -- I was trying to use a neutral term for how they were living there. They were existing there. That's where they were staying at the time, under, admittedly as described here, difficult conditions. It was nothing more than that. As Mr. Karnavas says, one step at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So there were both Muslims and Croats at the museum during this time period?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dear sir, we are going back to the same square one. You keep torturing me, torturing me, and then you draw a conclusion and you want me to say yes. While I was at the museum I didn't know there were any Muslims there. Only in 1994 when I got to Mostar, I found out that some Muslims had been there as refugees. All the people I had known about, because when entering the museum, I saw people from Doljani and elsewhere, and then I got down in the basement and I never got out again until the end. So my answer was: I didn't know there were any Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You see, that's -- again that wasn't my question, about what you knew at the time. You did find out, and you agree with me from what you found out, that there were Muslims and Croats in the museum at that time, and the answer to that apparently is yes, you did come to know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you said. You said yes. My answer is that I didn't know it while I was there. You didn't ask me what I found out in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I had earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Scott, I think you should --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Did you have something to say, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. It's been asked and answered. That's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's been asked -- one question has been asked, and the different answer has been given, but -- okay. Go, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I totally disagree with you, Judge Trechsel, on this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I don't mind. Please sit down, and, Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the nature of my questions, the tone of my questions has been fair. I'm just trying to seek clarification, and I don't think I've been pressing the witness unfairly, and I think that's clear to anyone in the courtroom, the questions I put in the last few minutes, so I'm not sure what the problem is. Let me see where we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in connection again with the museum, and again for clarification's sake, I hope I'm not pressing unfairly, but questions have come up, and in fact the President asked a question about this the other day and I'd like to come back to it to see if we can clarify the situation. If you have 1D 01859 available to you. I don't think it's -- I'm not sure if it's in the binder, but if we can have the assistance of the e-court please. 1D 01859. It's a document that, I believe, Mr. Karnavas showed to you. This was a list of people at the museum, a list of Croats at the museum dated the 16th of May, 1993. And perhaps -- I believe this was -- let me just make sure I'm not mistaken. You were listed as number 207, and your brother 208, I believe. 207 is Mirko Zelenika. 208 is Marko Zelenika. Now, this document is dated -- first of all, the document is dated the 16th of May, 1993. I don't know if there was an error in the date, but we understood -- or at least I had understood that you weren't kept at the museum until after the 8th of September, 1993. Can you clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said, sir, this was a list of people who were at the museum, but I'm telling you this is not the list of Croats who were in the museum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know what it is a list of, then? Again, so the record is clear, because we talked about on, I believe, Monday or Tuesday. What is it, please? When was this list prepared, for what purpose, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see the date on this list, and the purpose was to know exactly how many Croats in Jablanica were interned in some way, ghettoized, who were unable to leave until a certain point. Those were people who were still in Jablanica, in town, but not yet at the museum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So this goes back to the question that I was asking earlier about how many Croats were still in Jablanica around late April, early May 1993, but these were not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to be of assistance to everyone in the courtroom, including Mr. Scott. I believe there is a misunderstanding of what the witness is saying. If Mr. Scott wants to go back to paragraph 7 of the ECMM report, point 7 explains the document we're looking at now. The previous document, paragraph 7, will show why the witness is linking this current document to -- to what he's saying now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, Your Honour, and I don't know if the witness is linking it or not. I had understood and I appreciated the witness clarifying -- maybe I misunderstood from what was said previously, but now I understand that this is a list of civilians who were still in Jablanica, Croat civilians who were still in Jablanica town at that time period and not detained, because I thought the question that was put on -- hold on one moment. Because it's specifically in connection with this document. The testimony was and it was by the President, Your Honour, with great respect. Judge Antonetti said, "Was your brother detained with you in the museum? This morning we saw a list and he was in the list as you were." And that's where I was coming back to in connection with -- and that's the list that we were talking about at the time, 1D 01859.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So I think you've clarified further, sir, that this was not a list that was composed after you were put at the museum but as a list of civilians who were in Jablanica town in mid-May 1993. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I want to clarify something in addition to what my colleague Ms. Tomasegovic said. The title of the document we're looking at now, 1D 1859, relates also to Croats who are blocked in Jablanica. Not only the Croats who were detained but those who were blocked in Jablanica. Whereas the previous document, as I suppose my colleague wanted to say regarding paragraph 7 of the ECMM report, says that the Muslim refugees in Jablanica were enabled to leave Jablanica for Bugojno, whereas the Croats were isolated and prevented from evacuating. In that sense, they were Croats who were blocked in Jablanica without being detained yet. That's what the document, the previous document explains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was not making any of those links. I was simply asking for clarification. It seems like other counsel are conducting a different examination than the one that I'm conducting, but in any event, we've clarified the document. That was my only intention in terms of 1859.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On that point, say -- in terms of this testimony, excuse me, on this same point you referred to -- you said your brother was detained in Donja -- Donja Jablanica with Zuka, and then because of the consequences he suffered, he died in a camp. He was not at the museum. Judge Antonetti, question, "Did he die because of the consequences of his detention?" Witness: "Yes, that's what the doctors established." And just to be clear on that, sir, so was your brother ever detained at the museum or not and then moved someplace else, or was he never at the museum?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother was never at the museum. If you wish, I can clarify a bit more --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- concerning this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm trying to clarify that. No, please, I'm sorry. My time is limited. If I had more time, sir, we could talk about a lot of things a lot longer, I'm afraid, both of us. And your brother, unfortunately, then you said passed away at some point. As a -- as here he says -- well, Judge Antonetti's question was: "Did he die because of the consequences of his detention?" Can you tell us approximately when your brother passed away, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if you would stay away from questions about my brother. If you really want to know, in the clinical hospital of Mostar there are medical files in the internist department, but I'm not going to answer these questions any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, but the question was put to you before and you answered questions on this previously today, and I'm asking for clarification, and I've tried to do it in a very respectful way, I think, sir. All I'm asking is: Can you tell us the approximate date when your brother passed away? I'm sorry if that's difficult for you, but could you please give us the date?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He died five, six, or seven years later, but he had been in and out of hospital all that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of this questioning, this type of questioning, it does permit me, I believe, to go into details about what happened to this individual, this gentleman, as well as the brother, how they were tortured and how they were treated. We stayed away from that, but now we're getting into an area where it's far afield. I understand he's trying to impeach the gentleman as if he's confabulating or lying about his brother. That's what I believe is happening. But now I'm not permitted to go in because one of the Judges says, how can you do that, it's tu quoque. And quite rightly so to some degree. But now it appears -- now it appears that a door is being wide open, and the Trial Chamber needs to make a decision. At what point are they going to restrict the Prosecution to issues that are of relevance? I don't see anything from the Bench, and that's why I'm trying to intervene over and over again. And so I say -- I take it from your passivity that this is an area that we can go into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, to know the relevance one should know the Prosecutor's going to. I was listening to him. I was waiting to see what he wanted to underscore or highlight. Did he seek information on the death of the witness's brother? Did he want to test the witness's credibility? I know nothing about it. Just as when you ask questions sometimes I have no idea what you're aiming at, so I let you go, and then we draw conclusions. So here I don't know at all what the Prosecutor was trying to highlight. But, Witness, Mr. Karnavas said that you were tortured. We're not going to go into details, but you do confirm that it was a very painful, very difficult detention. That's what I understood, but I did not want to go into details, but your counsel is returning to this issue of your detention. So -- say your lawyer or counsel. Mr. Prlic's counsel returns to this issue. So it was a very difficult time this detention; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I find Mr. Karnavas's question as to the road you are taking and where you are heading quite justified. I had asked that before once today, but again could you -- could you explain us where this is supposed to lead?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm afraid this is a situation that everybody seems to be attributing some sort of an ulterior motive to me. I wanted to make sure -- and I'm not injecting a new issue. In fact I read to you, some moments ago, exactly some of the prior evidence from earlier this week. So Ken Scott did not initiate or raise this topic. So let's be very clear about that. And I've tried to be respectful and delicate with the issue, I think, but thought that it was -- it might be important at some point to know what we were talking about. And just as there were Muslims who were detained who had difficult conditions and may have died some years after, later, that could be the case, but I just thought -- I wanted to be clear whether this is something that happened at the time while he was -- while the brother was detained, as difficult as that would be, or was it something that happened some time later? And the witness has answered that question. I don't intend to pursue it any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As I said, Your Honour, that was exactly my intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with -- I'm changing topics here. Are you familiar with an organisation called the Association of Volunteers and Veterans of the Homeland War of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that is sometimes referred to, perhaps, and I don't know exactly how it would be translated, but UDIDDR? I've seen it both UDIDDR and also HDIDDR. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what the acronym stands for, but you cited the correct name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And have you been a member of that organisation, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall, sir, in 2000 being involved in a protest about the work of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember unless you help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could look, please, in the binder at P 10654. Sir, this is a news account of a -- what was described as a rally in January of 2000 that was apparently organised by the HBIDRA, and you were indicated as having been present, about the middle of the page. You should see it also in the Croatian version: "Mirko Zelenika, president of the Prisoners' Association of Mostar." The statement is attributed to you: "The political leadership of the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina must break its silence and define the aims of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Do you remember participating in this rally?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you ever taken a position, sir, or expressed a view on the creation or establishment of a separate Croat entity in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Some might have called it as the third entity.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that in connection with your testimony here and your role in the Jablanica municipality at the time, in fact you were one of the leading HVO activists in Jablanica municipality in 1992, 1993, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, you were one of the leading idealogues of the organisation, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By no means.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In connection with this rally in 2000, did you talk about the fact that every form of cooperation with the international community must be re-examined?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you that I can't confirm I was at that rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You can't -- are you saying you can't confirm and you're also not denying?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am denying. I wasn't there and I didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you ever talked about the holding of a referendum on the establishment of a Croat entity in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you ever discussed with anyone, in 2000, of defining the aims of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you express any view around this time, whether on that particular occasion or not but in January 2000 or in that time period, something along the lines that if the demands stated in this news item, if they -- if these demands are not met, we will -- we shall be held responsible by history and the Croat people which will be faced with its own extinction?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can just check on time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you -- before we leave at that document, sir, were you the president of the Prisoners' Association as indicated in this -- in that report around that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In 2000, sir, or 1999, 2000, 2001. During that general time period, had you been the president of something called the Prisoners' Association? And that may not be the full title, and if you were, perhaps you can assist us.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that period I was the president of the Croatian Association of Camp Inmates or Prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. All right. Sir, the final topic that I would like to turn to is questions that were put to you by various of the Defence counsel in connection with some additional events in April and May of 1993. Isn't it correct, sir, that the HVO actions that took place in Jablanica municipality in mid-April of 1993 were all part of an overall HVO plan arising or in connection with the HVO ultimatum that was given earlier that month with the 15 April deadline?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question is isn't it correct. Well, sir, it is absolutely not true, not correct what you say in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you had heard around that time of a decision issued by the HVO government to -- calling for this -- the ABiH to either leave the areas -- the Croat-controlled areas or subordinate themselves to the HVO by the 15th of April 1993, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this decision that you just mentioned is something that I've never heard of. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- let me stay with you a few moments longer and let me see if we can make any progress on that. Can I ask you to look at P 01808. P 01808.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where would it be?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We some assistance, please, Mr. Usher. P 01808.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So this is a news item for Borba, which I understand is a publication in Belgrade, and on the 5th of April, 1993, reporting in the second paragraph, it's from a -- excuse me. It's been reported -- the byline is Zagreb, and it says: "The Croatian Defence Council yesterday called for the pull-out of Muslim troops from the provinces assigned to the Croats under a UN peace plan thus heightening the tensions between the nominal allies. "The HVO command set April 15 as the deadline for Alija Izetbegovic to sign a joint document which calls for the pull-out of troops and the creation of a Joint Command, thus confirming that there are no disagreements between the Croats and Muslims. "If Izetbegovic does not sign the agreement by 15 April, the HVO will unilaterally establish its authority" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters. "Establish its authority in provinces 3, 8, and 10, says a communique from the HVO General Staff in Mostar. Croatian radio said yesterday that Bosnian Croat leader Mate Boban has signed the document and was waiting for the response of the Muslim authorities."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be allowed to object to this question. I would like to draw your attention to the fact that this is a report that was taken from the Croatian radio and published by Reuters, a British agency, and then it was published in a Belgrade daily, Borba. So this is just one media outlet retelling a story picked up from another media outlet, and I would like us to make sure that we all know that this is not the ultimatum itself. It is just a series of retelling of the story of the ultimatum from one media to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. No one ever said anything to the contrary. Again, I'm not sure what the objection is. It's a media article. If the Chamber would like to and if the courtroom would like to look at P 10675, you will see similar articles written on the 4th of April, 1993, in Reuters. Similar article in the Financial Times on the 20th of April, 1993. Similar article in the Christian Science Monitor on 7 April 1993. A similar article dated 6 April 1993 in the Agency French Press, Agence France Presse. And I won't pretend that my French is anything, but in the AFP. So counsel can pick any of the four or five articles she wants.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it correct that -- are you saying that you had never heard at the time, despite the fact that it was being reported around the world, that this deadline of April 15th, 1993, had been set?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that, sir. You have to know that we in Jablanica were in a media blockade too. We didn't read the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, in the course of -- in the course of the last few days you've told us, in fact, that you had the television. You listened to the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is this a legal objection or is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you want to say, Mr. Praljak? Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a legal objection. It's an objection because the Prosecutor keeps referring to the British and American media, the term that they -- that they broadcasted all over the world. Britain and the US are not the whole world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So stipulated, Your Honour. It's not the whole world but Financial Times, Reuters, AFP, are pretty widely disseminated news sources. All right. But we have -- in any event the witness says there was a blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But my question to you, sir, in response to that was, I thought you told us over the past several days that there was radio, there was television, that, in fact, these were all things that you were listening to in this time period. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. We are now in 1993, and in 1992 we were able to follow. We watched the TV, listened to radio and read the newspapers, but by 1993 we stopped watching TV and reading the papers and listening to the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And so even in the local news radio, because here it says, in the first document, P 01808, for example, says that: "A communique was issued by the HVO General Staff in Mostar." Some of us must might call that a press release. And then it goes on to say that: "Croatian radio said yesterday that Bosnian Croat leader Mate Boban had signed the document." So are you telling the Judges that, to your knowledge, no press releases or communiques from the HVO General Staff were being communicated around this time and that you were not getting Croatian radio around this time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I had listened to it, I would have heard something; but because I didn't listen, I didn't hear. And in particular, I did not hear anything of the sort of the thing that you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just try one more thing and then we'll see whether we pursue it further or not. Can I ask you to turn next to P 01911. P 01911. If you have that, sir. This is again an ECMM report titled, "The Present Jablanica Crisis." It is dated on the last page the 16th of April, 1993. And if I can direct your attention, please, to item number 3, which is titled, "Political Activity." Just one moment, please. My apologies. That relates to another part of my -- let me ask you to look to item 4, "Military Activity."

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you have that, sir. Excuse me a moment. My apologies. It's entirely my fault. My notes aren't correct, that I've made myself. Purely my fault. Let me try again. Item -- section number 6, which is titled "Indicators." My apologies to the courtroom. I had the document marked for a number of different purposes, and I went to the wrong place. Sir, in that section 6, and this is the particular aspect that I want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, this document P 1911 is deposited under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think it's one of those documents that we can use but should not be broadcast outside the courtroom. We can talk about it, but just so long as it's not being broadcast outside the courtroom, please. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in item 6 it says -- the second line says: "The HVO had declared their intent to implement the Vance-Owen Plan." Skipping down. In connection with the radio, that's the media that we've been talking in the last few minutes, it says: "The HVO make regular radio broadcast ultimatums to the Muslim forces in Herceg-Bosna (never written), yet seldom follow up the ultimatums suggesting that the concept is to provoke the Muslims into actions that can be used to justification for aggression in the name of defence." My point to you is not to argue the politics of it at this point, but again it says the regular radio broadcasts were made about these topics and about ultimatums. Now, just let me -- you don't recall any -- hearing any of that in any of the media, either in the print media or the electronic media, in the Jablanica area around this time? Sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, at that time I spent my time digging, from 7.00 until 4.30 in the afternoon. And even if I had wanted to, I wouldn't have been in a position to read anything or to listen to anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me check my notes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenika, in light of those answers, I won't persist in that particular line. I want to tell you again that none of my questioning was meant to cause you any particular pain or difficulty, but sometimes it may be difficult. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We should stop in ten minutes. Are there any redirect questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There are some, Your Honour. I can do it now or we could take a break. If we're going to be going past -- beyond -- if there are any other matters that we're going to be dealing with, then we could take the break. Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I know that Ms. Alaburic wants to talk about housekeeping questions. So the best would be to break now and you will redirect after the break, and we will talk about the housekeeping matters after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't believe I'll take more than five minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just three areas of clarification, sir. The first one deals with a document that was shown to you today, and that was P 10669, and I have it here. And this was in connection, of course -- if you could just look at that for a second. And, of course, today on page 4 it was noted, and I quote, this is on line 21: "Sir, you testified yesterday that you never received any salary or money in connection with working for MUP security station in Jablanica." Do you recall being asked that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We need the mics for the gentleman. The microphones, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let me show you this document -- if you could repeat the answer so we could get it on the record. Do you recall being asked that question today and shown this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's go back to a document that I showed you yesterday, and that was 1D 03038, and maybe if we can get the usher to help us out here so the gentleman doesn't have to look for it. Now, you recall me showing you this document. Now, this is dated, as we can see, 29 October 1992. This is from the Jablanica municipality Presidency, and we can see under Roman numeral II that you are temporarily sent to work in the public security station. Okay? Do you have that? Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I understand it -- if I understand your testimony correctly yesterday, when you said you did not receive a salary, that was in relation to this -- this decision and this appointment to temporary work at the public security station in Jablanica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the document that was shown to you today, of which you said you received from some -- some salary for work that was related to something other than police work, if we look at that document, and I don't know if it was missed but it certainly wasn't covered today, if we look at the first part -- first page, we see that this is from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it's the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna that is providing you with a salary for some 23 days of work that you did?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So when you said yesterday that you had not received a salary from the Jablanica municipality for the appointment of public security station Jablanica, the one that I just showed you, 1D 03038. You stand by that answer, correct, or do you wish to change it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. There seems to be -- I mean, the reason this was mentioned today was to suggest, perhaps, that you might have been confused or maybe you weren't quite truthful when you said that you never received a salary. And so I take it when you -- when you said you didn't receive a salary, that was for the appointment 1D 03038 with the Jablanica municipality Presidency appointing you to this temporary position.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. For this appointment I never got a salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just add a question which I find interesting. Witness, if one looks at this document, one gets the impression that there is a Jablanica police station which depends directly on Mostar and not at all to Jablanica municipality. Do I understand this correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no such thing as the Jablanica police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, it's Politsiska Stanica Jablanica. That does not exist according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Jablanica police station existed on this date, the 2nd of April -- is it 1993 or 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's 1993, according to the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1993, yes. But on the 29th of October, 1992, I was sent to the police station in Jablanica where I did not receive a salary and where I did not spend a long time, 15 days perhaps. Afterwards, I turned over all the documentation to Mostar, to the Herceg-Bosna police, and it was in the process of being resolved. I had no new appointment, but in the meantime, they were giving me some sort of pay. Since I had no appointment to the police, I was doing something else, and that something else was the supervision of works on road construction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we're limited in time. I could not say that it is absolutely clear to me, but I do not insist now because the time is limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me just ask one follow-up question, because there may be some confusion. As of this date on April 1993, is there an HVO or Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna police station in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all aspects of the police. There were no uniformed men. There were no police vehicles. This so-called police performed just a small fraction of administrative work such as collecting documents required for issuing Croatian passports. If you can call that police, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, you said collecting documents. Were they actually issuing Croatian passports or merely collecting the documents and then forwarding -- forwarding them onwards?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly didn't issue passports. They just physically collected these documents and carried them somewhere. I don't know where, perhaps to Mostar. I had nothing to do with the collecting of documents. I just received a small amount of money considering that I had already received some papers for the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, there was some questioning about Dr. Cibo and the legality of his appointment, and I brought it up. It was brought up on cross-examination. And I would like now for us to revisit a document that we really didn't discuss too much, and this is 1D 02777. And this is for clarification purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could get the usher to help us out here. This will save some time. It's 1D 02777. And that would be in the chapter dealing with civilian authorities, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you look at this document, we see that this is from Konjic municipality, and we see that this is from the president of the War Presidency, Dr. Rusmir Hadzihusejnovic. I think I got it right.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- and, in fact, before his name we see a Prim Doctor. I take it he is a medical doctor, right? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Primarius Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a title given or earned by doctors of high esteem, that have been recognised within the medical community for their abilities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very experienced medical doctors can get that title for special merits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could look at this document, because you were asked about the legality, and I'm going to focus your attention to paragraph number 2, in the middle of it. I'll read portions of it, and then I'll ask you to comment. It says here: "Accordingly, the War Presidency of the Municipal Assembly of Konjic was nominated pursuant to the decision number 10-042-9/92 of 26/10/1992 in the composition as provided for in paragraph 40 of the ordinance on defence with the force of law. In all the time since the formation, the War Presidency has been holding sessions and making decisions on the issues within the competence of the Municipal Assembly for the conditions of the Assembly to meet have not existed and still do not exist." Let's stop here for a second. Was the situation in Jablanica any different than what is being described by the president of the War Presidency in Konjic at this time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The situation in Jablanica was identical to the situation in Konjic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We go on. "We point out that the War Presidency, through its work, has been enforcing the regulations and other provisions of the Presidency of the republic, and those of the government and ministries, and has been performing the task specified in the defence plan of the republic." Let me stop here. Was Jablanica doing the same thing at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And now let's go to the final paragraph. "Considering the above stated, we fail to understand why the Presidency of the RB-H by the said decision should now appoint Dr. Cibo Safet president of the War Presidency of the Municipal Assembly of Konjic, considering that it was Prim Dr. Rusmir Hadzihusejnovic, the legally elected president of the Municipal Assembly of Konjic, who was elected president of the War Presidency in the municipality of Konjic, all pursuant to the ordinance on defence with the force of law." My final question is: In Jablanica was the war president also duly elected, legally elected, as was Dr. Rusmir Hadzihusejnovic in the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Jablanica the president of the War Presidency was elected legally, just as Mr. Rusmir Hadzihusejnovic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Finally, I just want to bring up one last item just for clarification purposes because there was a question from the Bench and -- yesterday, that is, concerning a list. 1D 1 -- 1859.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could get the usher to assist us here, I would be most grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is the list that was shown to you and that was -- you're on the list. You're on the list of -- your brother's on the list, and I believe your mother and father are on the list. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course, there was some confusion as to whether this was the list from the museum or whether it was just a list of Croats in Jablanica. And I believe at some point you -- you use a particular word that I thought was worth -- I jotted down and it caught my attention and I want you to explain it. You used the word "ghetto." Can you please tell us, what did you mean by that and what does it reflect, keeping in mind the time that this list was drawn up?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try. The thing is that from the arrival of Dr. Safet Cibo and from the beginning of the war between the army of BH and the HVO, all the Croats who found themselves on the territory held by the BH army were unable to leave the territory whether they wanted to seek medical treatment or they simply wanted to go. Some attempted to leave but they were caught and sent to the museum. So those who found themselves there had to do the trench digging like I did, and they were practically interned, isolated, or kept in a ghetto. Until 1994 they were unable to leave that area. I hope this explanation makes it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure we're clear, because the word "territory" was used and now "area." Are we speaking about a particular area within Jablanica where the Croats are being confined and they can't move out of there? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm talking about the area held by the BH army. All the Croats who found themselves in that area had no way of leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's why you characterised it as internment?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they had to do digging work like I did, or they were taken to the museum. There were also other camps in Jablanica. Some were sent to other camps. Simply due to the horrible situation in that area they were trying to leave in all possible ways, but it was impossible. The BH army wouldn't let them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One final question, because it came up today about your dissatisfaction with this institution, the Tribunal and its work. Yesterday I believe you told us, or it might have been the day before, that you did, in fact, assist investigators from this particular Tribunal in gathering evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for how many years did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us how often or how many times did you meet with these investigators to -- to assist them?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. An investigating team came to Mostar from this Tribunal at least 22 times in that three-and-a-half-year period. Each time they would stay three to five days. And my role was to meet their requests by securing the presence of persons they listed in advance, and these people were potential witnesses for specific cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And were you compensated? Were you paid for that work?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever complain that the Tribunal or the investigators weren't paying you for that work?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never asked them to be paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And finally, we understand that a statement was taken in -- with regard to one particular case, but you were never called; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The statement was taken, and I expected an invitation, but I never got the call.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the invitation you were expecting was because you wanted to tell your story about what had happened to you in addition to what you -- what you knew; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, in fact, you asked me if I could ask questions so that you would be allowed to tell your story, and I told you that that wasn't for this particular case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to thank you again, sir, for giving your testimony here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just add some questions to this last series. You said about three and a half years. Could you give us the beginning and end of this period, from when until when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you the precise time-frame. My first contact was with them in May 1995. Mr. Tom Kempenaars was the person. The investigation began in September 1995. The team leader was Mr. Abribat Regis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me if I interrupt you. I'm not asking about the names of the investigators. I take it the beginning of the three and a half years was in 1995. Did it then go through to 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the second question: When asked whether you were paid, you -- you did not simply answer no, but you said, "Not by the investigators," and this raises in me the question whether you were paid by anybody else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the centre for investigation and documentation in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On my own behalf and on behalf of my colleagues, I want to thank you for testifying, and for the Prlic Defence. If questions may have appeared to be difficult or tough, that's the rules and that's the proceedings as they are. Everyone asked the questions that they deemed necessary, and this is also why Judges put questions to you. If, unfortunately, this brought painful memories to the surface, we're very sorry for that. We wish you a very good trip back home, and I shall now ask the usher to escort you out of this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have a few housekeeping matters. Before I give the floor to Ms. Alaburic, let me say this: On the 27th of October, Mr. Karnavas is to start the testimony of Neven Tomic. On Monday, we will be starting at 9.00. So we'll work from 9.00 to 12.30, then from 2.00 to 2.30, I can't remember, until 4.00, because this courtroom is going to be used at 4.30 for a contempt case. So we'll start in the morning on Monday. That might be a problem for you if you have to proof the witness. No. It doesn't seem to be the case. So much the better. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I will really be very brief. The Honourable Trial Chamber made an oral ruling that you communicated to us today on page 1 of today's transcript; namely, that the part of my cross-examination of the witness who just left is to be considered as new issues, new questions, and in view of that the Trial Chamber will make the appropriate decision and deduct this time from the time allocated to the Petkovic Defence. Since this was a short oral ruling, it does not contain, of course, a statement of reasons. At first blush, I would say that it is not well founded because I would say these are not new issues but, rather, issues that are directly related to the answers of the witness on pages of the transcript from the 14th October, 40 to 41, answers namely related to document 1D 2758. The second reason that casts doubt on the appropriateness of this decision is the fact that the Prosecution recently received the right to open new questions according to Rule 90(H) under a recent decision of the Trial Chamber. Since this decision applies to both the Prosecution and the Defence, I believe it applies to the Petkovic Defence and the Prosecution, but if this right does not belong equally to all the Defence teams, I would like to know what the reasons for this decision of the Trial Chamber are. One the first prerequisites for an appellant appealing a decision is to review the reasons for the appeal, and I would appreciate it, therefore, if the Trial Chamber could put its oral ruling in writing stating the reasons, and then I would be able to assess whether it is correct ruling. And if I so decide after reviewing the reasons, I would apply for certification to appeal this decision. And that is all I had to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. The Trial Chamber will, of course, look into this and will keep you informed of whether we're going to have a written or oral decision. I can't give you an answer right now. Are there any other matters or topics? I'm turning to my right. No. Very well. We shall reconvene on Monday at 2.15. I wish you and Mr. Karnavas a good time working until then so that we can work as calmly as possible next week. See you on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 20th day of October, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.
